title: Basic Sales Vocabulary
subtitle: The everyday words sales and marketing teams use on the job
description: Learn eight everyday words sales and marketing professionals use at work — product, price, customer, buy, sell, discount, budget, and deal — as a new sales rep settles into the job.
dialogueSubtitle: Sam (sales manager) shows new sales rep Riley the basics of the job

vocabulary.definition: A thing or service that a company makes or sells.
vocabulary.example: Our project management app is the company's most popular product.
Could you remind me of the price for the premium plan?

vocabulary.definition: A person or company that buys something from a business.
vocabulary.example: We just signed a new customer — a marketing agency based in Toronto.

vocabulary.definition: To get something by paying money for it.
vocabulary.example: They've decided to buy the annual plan instead of paying monthly.

vocabulary.definition: To give something to someone in exchange for money.
vocabulary.example: Our team sells software to small and medium-sized businesses.
We're offering a 20% discount to anyone who signs up this quarter.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of money a person or company has to spend.
vocabulary.example: Before I recommend a plan, I always ask what their budget looks like.

vocabulary.definition: An agreement, especially in business, to buy, sell, or do something.
vocabulary.example: We closed three new deals with marketing agencies this month.

phrasalVerbs.definition: A friendly way to learn more about a potential customer's business.
phrasalVerbs.example: So, what does your company do? I'd love to learn more before we talk numbers.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: CAN I SHOW YOU HOW IT WORKS
phrasalVerbs.definition: Offer to give someone a quick demo of your product.
phrasalVerbs.example: Can I show you how it works? It only takes five minutes.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask how much money someone has to spend.
phrasalVerbs.example: Just so I can recommend the right plan — what's your budget?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Tell someone you'll email them the price for what they want.
phrasalVerbs.example: I'll send you a quote by the end of the day.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WE CAN OFFER YOU A DISCOUNT
phrasalVerbs.definition: Tell a customer you can give them a lower price.
phrasalVerbs.example: If you sign up this month, we can offer you a discount.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Tell someone you'll contact them again soon to continue the conversation.
phrasalVerbs.example: No problem — I'll follow up next week to see what you decide.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Welcome to the team! Our company sells software and cloud tools to other businesses — these are our [[products:things a company makes or sells]].

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Got it. So if a [[customer:a person or company that buys something from a business]] wants to try our software, I just explain how it works?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly! When a company wants to [[buy:to get something by paying money]] something, your job is to show them why our product is the right choice.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Should I ask about their [[budget:the amount of money a company has to spend]] before I suggest a plan?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Always. That leads straight into the [[price:how much money something costs]] talk — our starter plan is $49 a month, and the pro plan is $299.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: $299 a month? That's a big investment for a small business.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: True — that's why we're offering new customers a [[discount:a lower price than usual]] this quarter. 20% off the first year!

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Oh nice, so that brings it down to around $239 a month?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Always mention the discount early — it helps customers feel confident about saying yes.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Got it. And if I want to [[sell:to give something to someone in exchange for money]] more, I should just explain the benefits clearly?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: That's the secret. Know your product, listen to what the customer needs, and a good [[deal:an agreement to buy or sell something]] follows naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I think I'm ready. Let's go close some deals!

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in groups. Read the customer's line, then discuss which response (A, B, or C) is best. Choose your answer together, then click to see if you were right — and why.

options: It's expensive, but it's worth every penny.
The price depends on what you need. What's your budget?
We have lots of different products — I'll send you our full catalogue.
items.explanation: B is correct. Asking about budget before quoting a price shows you want to find the right fit. A sounds dismissive. C avoids the question and sends the customer away.

items.customerLine: Can you give me a discount?
options: How much of a discount are you looking for?
If you sign up this month, we can offer you a 20% discount.
items.explanation: C is correct. It offers a discount with a clear condition, which is professional and creates urgency. A shuts the conversation down. B gives the customer too much control over the price before you have established the product's value.

items.customerLine: I need to think about it.
options: Of course — I'll follow up next week to see what you decide.
Are you sure? This is a really great deal.
OK, no problem. Let me know when you're ready.
items.explanation: A is correct. It keeps the conversation alive with a specific next step. B is pushy and could damage the relationship. C is polite but too passive — there is no clear plan to continue.

items.customerLine: What exactly does your company sell?
options: We sell lots of different things — it depends on what you need.
Check our website — everything is listed there.
We sell software to businesses. Can I show you how it works?
items.explanation: C is correct. It gives a clear, confident answer and immediately offers the next step. A is too vague. B sends the customer away instead of keeping them engaged.

profileMatch.instructions: Read the three customer profiles. As a group, match each customer to the plan that best fits their needs. Be ready to explain your choices using words from this lesson. Click 'Reveal Matches' to check.

profiles.name: Kenji
profiles.description: Kenji runs a 2-person freelance design studio. He has a very small budget and just needs a simple way to track projects and invoice his customers.

profiles.name: Amara
profiles.description: Amara manages a team of 15 at a growing marketing agency. She wants to track deals, manage customer relationships, and see reports on what her team is selling.

profiles.name: David
profiles.description: David is IT director at a 200-person company. He needs a fully custom solution that connects with their existing systems and comes with a dedicated support team.

options.label: Starter Plan — $49/month
options.description: Basic project tracking and invoicing. Up to 5 users. Best for small teams or freelancers who need a simple, low-cost tool.

options.label: Growth Plan — $149/month
options.description: Deal tracking, customer management, and reporting. Up to 25 users. Best for growing teams that need to manage relationships and track results.

options.label: Enterprise Plan — Custom pricing
options.description: Unlimited users, custom integrations, dedicated account manager. Best for large companies that need a fully tailored solution.
